title: Each species arose in a single area and spread from there

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Each species arose in a single area and spread from there

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Each species was first produced in one area only and subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence allowed under past and present conditions, rather than arising independently at several points.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Hence it seems to me, as it has to many other naturalists, that the view of each species having been produced in one area alone, and having subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence under past and present conditions permitted, is the most probable.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XI, “Geographical Distribution”; section “Centres of creation”. Scope: all species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch11-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.66

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern phylogeography can strongly test selected species. Data are not adequate across all species, and deep origins are often non-identifiable from present descendants alone.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For species with dense genomic and occurrence sampling, infer ancestral geographic origin and expansion history and test monophyly of populations against independent polycentric origins. Repeated well-supported single origins would support the generalization.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A single-origin model can be difficult to distinguish from gene flow after multiple origins.

Species boundaries and geographic origins are often uncertain.

Extinction erases source populations.

analysis feasibility: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.58
data existence: 0.83
discriminating power: 0.5

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Single versus multiple origin is a standard phylogeographic hypothesis, and public sequences exist for thousands of species. That is a large subset and far from all species. Where sampling is dense, multiple unrelated origins are distinguishable from spread of one population, so the limit is coverage and compilation time.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For species with range-wide genetic sampling, ask whether gene trees fit one ancestral area followed by spread, or require two or more unrelated origins. A substantial share of species with well-supported multiple origins would challenge the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Range-wide sequences exist for a small fraction of species.

Cryptic species and over-lumped names can look like multiple origins of one species.

Published phylogeographies would have to be compiled, which is months of work at global scope.
